notes.meaning: Isaiah asks who has truly believed the message spoken by God's messengers. God showed His mighty power—called here the arm of the Lord—in a way so unexpected and humble that few recognized it. Most people looked for worldly majesty and failed to see God at work in His Servant.

The Servant grew up quietly like a small, fragile plant springing out of dry ground. He did not come with royal splendor, wealth, or striking physical beauty to impress people. Because He appeared so ordinary and plain, the crowds saw nothing outward to draw them to Him.

People despised the Servant and pushed Him away as if He were worthless. He was deeply familiar with sorrow, pain, and grief throughout His life. Instead of showing Him honor, people hid their faces in disgust and treated Him as nothing.

The Servant took our sicknesses, pains, and griefs upon Himself as His own burden. People who saw Him suffer assumed God was angry with Him and striking Him down for His own wrongs. In truth, He was bearing the painful weight of our troubles in our place.

The Servant was pierced through and crushed for our sins, suffering the penalty we deserved. The punishment He took brought us peace, which means wholeness and a restored relationship with God. By His painful wounds, we are healed from the guilt and ruin of sin.

differ.view: Deliverance from bodily sickness is provided in Christ's atonement for believers today, although full physical restoration is completed when Christ returns.
Christ's wounds purchase both spiritual forgiveness and physical healing, but bodily healing is not guaranteed in every case in this life and reaches its full reality at the resurrection.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Because Christ was wounded for our healing, every Christian is promised complete physical health right now, and persistent sickness shows a failure to claim that promise in faith.

notes.meaning: Like foolish sheep that wander away from their shepherd, all people have turned away from God to chase their own selfish paths. We could not save ourselves from the danger of our lost condition. Yet the Lord gathered the full guilt and punishment of our sins and laid them entirely upon His Servant.

The Servant suffered harsh abuse and oppression, yet He remained silent and never complained or defended Himself. Like a gentle lamb being led away to slaughter, He willingly obeyed His Father's will. Even in the face of death, He stayed calm and chose not to fight back.

An unjust trial and cruel violence dragged the Servant away to be killed in midlife. People of His time did not realize that He died without physical heirs or legal defense. He was cut off from the land of the living so that He could take the fatal blow meant for God's people.

His enemies planned for Him to be thrown into a dishonorable grave alongside wicked criminals. Instead, He was placed in the tomb of a rich man after His death. This honor was fitting because He was entirely innocent, never doing any violence or speaking any deceitful words.

The Lord chose to allow His Servant to be crushed and suffer because it was part of His wise plan to rescue sinners. When the Servant offered His own life as a guilt offering to pay for sin, death would not be the end. He would live again, seeing a massive family of spiritual children and bringing God's good plan to complete success.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God permitted the Servant to suffer as part of His loving plan rather than actively punishing Him with divine wrath, viewing His death as a voluntary sacrifice that pays man's debt.

notes.meaning: After enduring the deep agony of His soul, the Servant sees the fruit of His labor and is fully satisfied. Through knowing Him, this righteous Servant will justify many, which means declaring them right with God. He accomplishes this because He takes their sins upon Himself.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Bearing iniquities does not mean Christ took on personal guilt or legal punishment, but that He offered a loving sacrifice to wipe away sin on humanity's behalf.

notes.meaning: God honors the Servant with a glorious reward, treating Him like a victorious king who shares the spoils of triumph. This great honor comes because He willingly poured out His life unto death and was counted among lawbreakers. In doing so, He carried the sins of many people and prayed for the very rebels who sinned against God.
